subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Attentional Blink
description: Learn The Attentional Blink in one minute.

hook.text: Flash letters on a screen, one every tenth of a second. Spot the first target? Easy. Spot the second? Gone.

buildup.text: For about 200 to 500 milliseconds after spotting a target, your brain goes temporarily blind to the next one.

discovery.text: This is the attentional blink—a bottleneck in conscious awareness, not in perception itself.

twist.text: The second target hits your retina and is partly processed. You just can't bring it to awareness.

climax.text: Meditators show shorter blinks. Training can shrink the gap between what you see and what you notice.

punchline.text: Awareness has a refractory period—like a camera flash recharging.

details.summary: When two targets appear in rapid succession within a stream of items, the second target is often missed if it appears 200 to 500 milliseconds after the first. This attentional blink reveals a temporary blind spot in awareness during the processing of the first target.
details.whyItMatters: The attentional blink demonstrates that conscious awareness has a refresh rate. Processing one meaningful event temporarily blinds us to the next, with real implications for reading, monitoring, and rapid decision-making.
takeaways: The second of two rapid targets is often missed
The blind window lasts about 200 to 500 milliseconds
Emotional or personally relevant targets reduce the blink

faq.question: Can the attentional blink be reduced?
faq.answer: Meditation training, positive mood, and reducing the importance placed on the first target can all shrink the attentional blink. Some individuals naturally show a smaller blink. The effect is robust but not entirely fixed, suggesting some flexibility in temporal attention.

faq.question: What does the attentional blink tell us about consciousness?
faq.answer: It suggests that conscious awareness requires time to consolidate each event. During consolidation of the first target, the gate to awareness temporarily closes. This supports theories that consciousness operates in discrete episodes rather than as a continuous stream.
